title: Christ's suffering, exaltation, and the one power of God
english: Continuing with the words of the comparison, he says, "I have become like those who have been slain and lie in a tomb" (Psalm 87:6 (88:5)). They suffer this because they were separated from your life-giving power. For it is clear that this was not true of him. The body of Christ was full of the power of God even after death. That is why blood and water flowed from him, something that never comes from dead bodies.

Another, explaining the words "You have made me an abomination to them" (Psalm 87:9 (88:8)), says: Just as the disciples were ashamed at his sufferings, no longer hoping for a Savior or redeemer—they even said, "The rulers handed him over to a sentence of death, but we had hoped that he was the one who was going to redeem Israel" (Luke 24:21). It is clear that he was also held fast in the hands of his enemies, handed over willingly, yet still held. There he came into affliction for our sake. For he bore everything that is heavy and afflicting to a body. For instead of "My eyes have grown weak from poverty" (Psalm 87:10 (88:9)), Symmachus rendered, "My eye has poured out from affliction."

Save, then, the race you have made, by your own knowledge, and lead back to life the human beings who have fallen into death in each way (Ps 87:13). They must be spectators of your wonders and interpreters of your power. Let them not remain overlooked in forgetfulness, but let them be remembered again by you and led back to life. This is what the champion of human beings says, interceding for the common race of all and working out the life of the world by the will of the Father.

The ambassador and priest presents himself on our behalf with unceasing presentation, from dawn and through the night, and he appeases the wrath of God against us, which he himself took upon himself in his sufferings (Ps 87:14).

He calls "exaltation" the exaltation in wonders and signs, about which the Father says to him, "I have glorified it" (John 12:28), while the Son says, "Glorify your Son" (John 17:1) (Ps 87:16). He says this was changed into humiliation when he came to suffer, suffering for human beings and abandoned by them, the ones for whom he suffered.

Mount Tabor lies in the region of the Galileans, and Hermon in the desert near Sinai (Ps 88:13). God must be hymned, he says, not only for his works around Tabor but also for the manifestation that took place around Hermon.

"Your power," he says, "prevails" (Ps 88:14-15). Let your strength appear, let it become manifest and glorious among human beings. All these things he has included as spoken to one God. We know his power as one and only, and his arm and hand as perfect. Through it all things have come into being and are coming into being, so that it, being perfect in itself, is numbered with God according to the one number of divinity, and in no way falls into what is said about the many sons, none of whom the word has said beforehand is like the true one. For the one true power is not like that, but is uniquely the true image and mark of God, God accomplishing all things through it. Therefore the divine things were fitted to its sojourn among human beings, and the judgment of God is dispensed by Christ. This power exists as the power of God, but was given as to a human being, as Christ himself said, and God divided mercy and judgment by the times. He foretold the judgment from then on, when the king comes and sits on the throne of his glory. For that throne has righteousness as its foundation, as Aquila also said beforehand in the ninth psalm: "He set his throne in judgment" (Psalm 9:8 (9:7)). Before that manifestation, mercy was abundant on the earth, like a forerunner of the critical coming, as the fearful judge who is about to appear prepares human beings for salvation by mercy. And with mercy comes truth, because it is not possible for anything untrue or not upright to occur in God's good patience, even if it seems to those who do not know the future that the wicked are wrongly allowed to prosper, nor is it reasonable that the good are overlooked when they suffer loss.

He now explicitly recounts the promise made through Nathan the prophet, indicating prophets in the plural from one, whom he also calls sons of God, or as the other interpreters render it, holy ones of God (Ps 88:20-25).

orientation: Apollinaris continues his verse-by-verse exposition of Psalm 87 (88) and begins Psalm 88 (89), interpreting the psalmist's words as spoken in the person of Christ and explaining the one divine power shared by Father and Son.

title: God's promise to David and the hope of resurrection
english: He says that God declared he had shared his power with David and brought him forward into glory, choosing him according to the words, "I took you from the sheepfold, from behind the flocks, to be leader over my people Israel" (2 Samuel 7:8). And when he found him pleasing, he anointed him with holy oil for the kingdom. God was present with him, working together with him in everything, making the uprisings of his enemies ineffective, shattering their armies, and putting them to flight, according to the words, "I was with you in all that you undertook, and I destroyed all your enemies before your face" (2 Samuel 7:9) (Ps 88:36). These things were spoken through Nathan the prophet. He says that David was exalted by the mercy that is from God and by the care that is fitting toward the righteous man, just as he also won victories in wars beyond all expectation and was undefeated.

God swears by himself, since he has no one greater by whom to swear, as Paul says. For he says, "I swore by my holiness," or as the Fifth Edition renders it, "By my sanctification," instead of "By my holiness" (Psalm 88:36 (89:35)) (Ps 88:39). [On Psalm 88:39–46 (89:38–45): Theodoret set out these things in the same way as Apollinaris.]

He appears to be seeking something greater and beyond human capacity, belittling the life we now live as being nothing (Ps 88:49). He says that human beings pass into something vain—not that they came into being for vanity—and he asks that they not be handed over to corruption, since clearly the kingdom will also be restored then, when corruption is dissolved and life for the ages is given. From where could escape from death come to us? From where, except from you? For this could not come to a human being from himself. No one exists who will live and not die, nor will anyone be able to rescue himself from death. These words plainly seek the heavenly king, the redeemer from vanity, the one who is stronger than death and the Savior of human beings from death, who changes the vanity of the present life into truth and establishes an eternal kingdom upon eternal life.

He did not despair of mercy, but he seeks the promise and calls upon the righteousness of God against the impious nations who reproach the righteous man for having suffered misfortune in his offspring and having fallen (Ps 88:51). He says these are enemies of God, and they reproach the footprint of the righteous king as if it had been wiped out. After making these appeals, he blesses. The blessing belongs to one who hopes. And what does he hope for, except that the prayers will be fulfilled, that the promise will be accomplished and not fail, as he appears to have believed from the beginning? As Paul also says, "It is not as though the word of God has failed" (cf. Romans 9:6).
If he has spoken this way about a thousand years, it is clear that the span of a human life will be the thinnest possible, as if indivisible (Ps 89:10).

The whole of human life, he says, is bounded by about seventy years. He says this from the greater part. And not even this is given in ease, but almost entirely in hardship. For either we are disciplined as infants, or we labor as young men, or we suffer hardship as old men. So he rightly said, "And the greater part of them is labor and pain" (Psalm 89:10 (90:10)) (Ps 89:17). For since the order of life follows age in this way, very little time is found that is stolen away for gladness.

He fittingly called this entire time "night," in which a human being sleeps while being put to death, and "morning" the time that is coming, in which we will live when the Lord appears and mercy comes down from heaven. He asks that the sun come and the day shine forth, and that enduring gladness be given to the righteous in place of the days in which we were afflicted, falling into countless evils. These were the times of refreshing that Peter also foretells, into which he says the appointed Jesus our Lord will be sent (Acts 3:20).

Next he says that a thousand will fall on the left and ten thousand on the right, before they can even draw near and inflict any harm, so that he will look without fear, by the recompense from God, upon those falling and being destroyed (Ps 90:8). This is what happened to Jehoshaphat according to the promise, so that without fighting—but singing and praising God through one another—he saw the enemies destroyed. For it says, "They came to the watchtower of the wilderness and looked and saw the multitude, and behold, all were dead, fallen on the ground, and there was no one saved" (2 Chronicles 20:24). Something similar to this also happened with other kings who hoped in God, as the promise of God proved true, which says, "I will be an enemy to your enemies and oppose those who oppose you" (Exodus 23:22). But one must not always suppose that victories come to the righteous without battle. For they often won by going through battle as well, but he speaks here of the most manifest help, in which God the helper is especially seen (Ps 90:9).

He introduced the person of the one who hopes, saying from himself to God that he has made him his hope. And again he declares to such a person: "Since you have chosen the Most High like a house of security, you will be mastered by no evil, nor will your house be struck by divinely sent blows" (Ps 90:10).

orientation: Apollinaris is commenting on Psalm 88 (89), explaining how God's promise to David through Nathan the prophet was fulfilled in David's victories, and then how the psalmist's lament over human mortality points to the heavenly king who rescues from death.

title: The righteous suffer as training, not punishment; God's justice overthrows the wicked
english: For it is clear that if a righteous person suffers anything, and the house of a righteous person too, this is a contest from the unrighteous who oppose them, and not a punishment from God. It is also clear that evils will not overpower the one who suffers in the manner of training, but he will rise up as from sleep, just as it was said in the third psalm (Psalm 3); and if he falls seven times, according to the proverb, he will rise again (Proverbs 24:16) (Ps 92:1b; Prov 24:16).

It is possible, then, to speak of putting on glory and girding on power with reference to what is known among human beings, but it is more fitting to speak of it with reference to the dishonor that came to Christ in his first coming and to his human weakness. He himself leads the world, made firm in him for secure good things, which it is no longer possible to move in any way.

It is not possible, he says, for unjust kingdoms to share in your power, which bring toil on those who keep the law, by whom the righteous person is hunted for arrest and the one who does no wrong is murdered (Ps 93:20). In these words he shows altogether the overthrow of injustice, which is established by the righteousness of God. You will not give power to the wicked, he said, but you will place security around the righteous person, standing as a stronghold for him and strengthening his hopes in you. And what the wicked thought would succeed for them against the righteous, these things will turn back and come upon themselves; and as they plotted to make the righteous invisible, so they will go away into invisibility. This is the end of the vengeance that comes from you.

Let the God whom we worship be known, the one who has heaven and the glory above heaven, to whom beauty is present, to whom power and majesty belong in secret—according to his incorporeal and divine excellence, since the bodily sizes and beauties of temples have been produced with technical precision and lavish wealth, and for the nations they are for demons (Ps 95:6). But in Israel, even if these things were present, they had come into being from the beginning as a type of the invisible things, and it was said through Moses, and they yield to the invisible things—especially now in the present proclamation of the gospel, when spiritual majesty is sought and contemplated, but also in ancient times among the wise, as with Solomon, who said that he was building a temple for God as the greatest and most lavish, since God is the greatest, yet also said that not even heaven can contain the glory of God (Ps 96:1).

The words "The Lord reigned" must be heard in one way just now and in another way now. For from his first coming he reigned, as in a summary, condemning sin in his holy flesh and abolishing death; and in his second coming he will reign through each one of those who share in him, having destroyed evil and corruption, when people will come to behold the steward of eternal life, being already able to be filled with life from him and to behold the glory of his kingdom, which is manifested in them as in a royal house, and which makes the opponents invisible as fire melts wax (Ps 96:7-8). So he says again that the earth rejoices and the many islands are glad—that is, the nations—and then next that the earth is in labor and the mountains melt. In one place he speaks of the saints, and in another of the opponents, whose height through pride he likens to mountains, and he compares the overthrow of their pride to the melting of mountains. And to those who are alien he shows cloud and darkness meeting them before the sight of the Lord, signifying fear and distress; but to those who are receptive to light he says his lightnings flash and his glory is seen, and also that the fire of judgment will consume the ungodly, when the righteousness of the Lord is revealed from heaven, as the apostle says. And the psalmist says that the revelation from heaven is announced by the heavens, calling the manifestation an announcement, and he says that heaven itself is established by righteousness and judgment as on some support. He makes it clear that the throne is not bodily, but that the kingdom is called a throne.

He prays that those who through great insensibility and foolishness worship the images which they themselves carved may be put to shame, having received perception. For such a thing will be for their good. For being put to shame, they will depart from this foolish opinion which they held as if about gods.
Evil is opposed and hostile to God, though not by any opposition in nature.

orientation: Apollinaris is commenting on Psalm 91 (92), explaining that the righteous person's afflictions come from enemies as discipline, not from God as punishment, and then moves to Psalms 92-96 (93-97) on God's majesty, judgment, and the overthrow of the wicked.
